label: Mind
title: Mind in the head
description: This was the free-response result for mind in a study recruiting 206 Rutgers students. Participants also selected locations on a body diagram.
limit: These are reported beliefs in one student sample, not observed spontaneous gestures or a cross-cultural census.

label: Self
title: Self has more than one reported location
finding: 40.5% named head, brain or mind; 12.7% named heart or chest.
description: These are selected free-response categories. Another 22.4% named the body without specifying one region.
limit: Other responses are not plotted. These percentages describe this study’s respondents, not the world.

label: Soul
title: Soul often moves toward the chest
finding: 42.0% named heart or chest; 22.0% named head, brain or mind.
description: These are selected free-response categories from the same study. Changing the term changed the pattern of answers.
limit: Other responses included the body generally and no bodily location. This does not establish that a soul has a physical location.

label: Pointing to self
title: An actual pointing task
finding: Self-location judgments clustered around head and upper torso.
description: Participants adjusted a pointer toward themselves while blindfolded, or judged its alignment visually. The study asked about the self.
limit: This is a structured experiment, not a study of spontaneous gestures for the word “mind.”

label: 마음 · maeum
title: Korean 마음: a gesture toward the heart
finding: People point to the heart when referring to maeum.
description: Matty Wegehaupt reports this gesture from his experience in Korea. The word 마음 includes mind and heart, as well as intention and will.
limit: The gesture is a contributor’s observation. The dictionary supports the word’s senses; it does not establish how often or how widely the gesture occurs.

label: ASL · MIND
title: A sign toward the upper head
finding: The forefinger points toward the side of the upper head.
description: HandSpeak documents this form for MIND. A sign’s location is part of how the language expresses meaning.
limit: The sign does not by itself reveal a signer’s theory of consciousness. ASL is distinct from other signed languages.

label: Egypt · heart
title: Heart, mind and memory
finding: The heart has a place in accounts of mind and memory.
description: The British Museum’s Greenfield Papyrus record connects these aspects of a person with the heart, within a funerary and religious setting.
limit: This textual evidence is not an observation of how ancient Egyptians pointed to themselves.

label: Chinese · 心
title: Heart and thinking in 心
finding: Xīn connects the bodily heart and thinking.
description: The Chinese Text Project dictionary records these related senses. “Heart-mind” keeps the connection visible in translation.
limit: A lexical record does not establish a pointing custom or one doctrine shared by all Chinese traditions.
